Linear Time Subsequence and Supersequence Regex Matching

**Abstract**

It is well-known that checking whether a given string _w_ matches a given regular expression _r_ can be done in quadratic time \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\) and that this cannot be improved to a truly subquadratic running time of \(O((|w|\cdot|r|)^{1-\epsilon})\) assuming the strong exponential time hypothesis (SETH). We study the related problem that asks whether _w_ has a _subsequence_ that matches _r_, and we show that surprisingly this task admits an algorithm that runs in linear time, i.e., in _O_(|_w_|+|_r_|). We further show that the same holds if we ask for a supersequence instead of a subsequence. Moreover, we show that the _quantitative_ problems of computing a longest subsequence or shortest supersequence of _w_ that matches _r_ can be solved with the same complexity as the classical longest common subsequence or shortest common supersequence problems, i.e., in \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\), and conditionally not in \(O((|w|\cdot|r|)^{1-\epsilon})\).

By contrast, if instead of subsequences or supersequences we consider other string relations like the infix, prefix, left-extension, or extension relations, then all the corresponding problems (both quantitative and non-quantitative) have the same complexity as classical regex matching, i.e., they can also be solved in \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\), but not in \(O((|w|\cdot|r|)^{1-\epsilon})\) assuming SETH.

We last study the complexity of the _universal_ problem that asks if _all_ subsequences (or supersequences, infixes, prefixes, left-extensions or extensions) of an input string satisfy a given regular expression. For these problems, we show polynomial upper bounds (along with matching conditional lower bounds) for the infix and prefix relations, but PSPACE-completeness for the extension, left-extension and supersequence relations, and coNP-completeness for the subsequence relation.

## 1 Introduction

Regular expressions (also called regex) were first introduced by Kleene in 1956 [Kle56] as a theoretical concept and quickly found their way into practice with the classical construction by Thompson [Tho68]. <tbc>standard textbook \[Fri06\]). The most important problem about regular expressions is their _matching problem_, i.e., checking whether a given regular expression _r_ matches a given string _w_. One of the two main algorithmic approaches to this problem is still Thompson’s original construction: transform _r_ into a nondeterministic finite automaton with \(\varepsilon\)-transitions (or \(\varepsilon\)NFA) _A_ in linear time, and then simulate _A_ on _w_ in time \(O(|w|\cdot|A|)\). (The other approach is to transform _r_ into a deterministic finite automaton or DFA, whose size is generally exponential in _r_.)

In addition to their well-known applications as text analysis tools, regular expressions are also used in many different areas and are at the core of several data management principles: graph databases \[AAB<sup>+</sup>17\], information extraction \[FKRV15\], complex event processing \[GRUV21\], network monitoring \[LN19\], financial fraud detection \[SK15\], infrastructure security \[KCTV07\], etc. The problem of regular expression matching (and the strongly related problem of NFA acceptance) is also one of the base problems investigated in fine-grained complexity \[BI16, BGKL24, BGL17\]. A classical result in this area is that the long-standing quadratic upper bound of \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\) for matching is optimal in the sense that it cannot be improved to truly subquadratic complexity of \(O((|w|\cdot|r|)^{1-\epsilon})\) unless the _strong exponential time hypothesis_ (SETH) fails: see \[BI16\].<sup>1</sup>

We contribute to the research on regex matching by exploring the following new angle. Instead of asking whether the whole input string _w_ matches the regex _r_, we ask whether _w_ has a _subsequence_ that matches _r_; or a _supersequence_ that matches _r_; or, more generally, whether _r_ matches some string _u_ with \(u\unknown w\), where \(\unknown\) is a fixed string relation (and classical regex matching is then the case when \(\unknown\) is the equality relation). While technically any possible string relation \(\unknown\) instantiates a \(\unknown\)-version of the regex matching problem, we focus on relations that are relevant for string matching: the subsequence relation (\(x_1x_2\dots x_n\unknown_\text{sub}w\Leftrightarrow w=w_0x_1w_1x_2\dots x_nw_n\)), supersequence relation (\(u\unknown_\text{sup}w\Leftrightarrow w\unknown_\text{sub}u\)), infix relation (\(u\unknown_\text{in}w\Leftrightarrow w=vuv'\)), prefix relation (\(u\unknown_\text{pre}w\Leftrightarrow w=uv\)), left-extension relation (\(u\unknown_\text{text}w\Leftrightarrow u=vw\)), and extension relation (\(u\unknown_\text{ext}w\Leftrightarrow w\unknown_\text{in}u\)).

## 1.1 Our Results

Our main focus is on the subsequence and supersequence relations, and our first contribution is to show that the complexity of regular expression matching can be substantially improved when performed with these relations. Namely, we show that given a regex _r_ and string _w_, we can check in time _O_(|_w_|+|_r_|) whether some subsequence of _w_ matches _r_, or whether some supersequence of _w_ matches _r_. We believe that this tractability result is quite surprising, and it turns out to be in strong contrast to the same problem for other string relations (infix, prefix, left-extension and extension), or for regex matching in the usual sense. Indeed, in all these cases, we show that the complexity of \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\) is optimal in the sense explained above (assuming SETH).

Our linear time upper bound for subsequence and supersequence matching is achieved by transforming the regex _r_ into an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_ that accepts _w_ if and only if _w_ has a subsequence (or supersequence) that matches _r_, following a known construction in the context of so-called upward and downward closures \[BLS15\]. We then exploit special properties of _A_ that allow us to decide whether it accepts _w_ in linear time. It is then not very difficult to improve the bound and make it linear in the input word: however, more effort is needed to also ensure that the complexity is linear in the regex (in particular in the setting where the input alphabet is not constant), and achieve the optimal complexity of _O_(|_w_|+|_r_|).

Motivated by this positive algorithmic result, we investigate a natural generalisation of the matching problem: compute a maximum-length/minimum-length string _u_ with \(u\unknown w\) that matches _r_. However, it turns out that our linear time algorithm for subsequence and supersequence regex matching does not generalise to this stronger problem, and we can in fact show that subquadratic algorithms for these min- and max-variants are conditionally not possible. More precisely, for the max-variant of the subsequence relation or the min-variant of the supersequence relation, we show that truly subquadratic algorithms would imply truly subquadratic algorithms<tbc>

For the min-variant of the subsequence relation or the max-variant of the supersequence relation, we show that a truly subquadratic algorithm would imply a faster algorithm for the Orthogonal Vectors problem, which is also impossible under SETH \[ABDN18, Wil05\]. On the positive side, however, we show that all these problems can be solved within the original matching complexity of \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\), in particular generalising the fact that longest common subsequences and shortest common supersequences can be computed within this bound. We also show that the same upper bounds apply for the infix, prefix, and (left-)extension relations, and that they are all optimal under SETH.

In this regard, it is worth noting that both the max-variant for the subsequence relation and the min-variant for the supersequence relation properly extend the classical regex matching problem, since a matching maximum-length subsequence _u_ or minimum-length supersequence _v_ equals _w_ if and only if \(w\in\mathsf{L}(r)\). In fact, we could interpret _u_ and _v_ as a fuzzy measure for regex matching: The tighter _w_ is sandwiched in between _u_ and _v_, the more it can be interpreted as matching the regex _r_, where the optimum _u=v=w_ is reached when \(w\in\mathsf{L}(r)\).

Finally, we investigate the complexity of checking whether _all_ strings _u_ with \(u\unknown w\) match _r_. While it is easy to see that this can be solved efficiently for the infix and prefix relations, it becomes intractable for the (left-)extension, subsequence and supersequence relations. We pinpoint the complexity of all these variants (conditionally on SETH).

See s 1 and 2 for an overview of all our upper and lower complexity bounds.

Moreover, algorithmic problems related to the analysis of the set of subsequences of the strings of a formal language, given as a grammar or automaton, are studied in \[AFH<sup>+</sup>25\] and \[FKM<sup>+</sup>24\]. Closer to our topic, matching regular expressions to the subsequences of a string is an important paradigm in event stream processing, where we receive a stream of events that result from different processes, and where consecutive events from the same process are represented as a subsequence in this string (see, e.g., \[AMU<sup>+</sup>17, GAA<sup>+</sup>20, ZDI14, KSS<sup>+</sup>22, KSS<sup>+</sup>23, FK23, GRUV21\]).

Our results can also be interpreted as providing a new angle to study the fine-grained complexity of the regex matching problem. In particular, the classical paper of Backurs and Indyk \[BI16\], which initiated the study of the fine-grained complexity of regex matching, investigates the following question: for which regex classes can the quadratic upper bound for matching be improved, ideally to linear time _O_(|_w_|+|_r_|), and for which classes is this impossible (assuming SETH). This question is further studied in \[BGL17\]. In these works, the restricted classes are defined as _homogeneous_ regex, i.e., where the operators used at each depth of the formula are all equal. In the present paper, we carry out a similar study, but instead of restricted regex classes, we consider different matching paradigms: we identify string relations for which regex matching becomes linear time solvable and others for which this is conditionally not the case. However, we can also understand our results as giving a linear time bound on the class of regex defining so-called _upward-closed_ and _downward-closed_ languages, as we will explain later.

In addition to investigating how the regex matching problem could be restricted in order to obtain subquadratic variants (either classically by restricting the class of input regex or, as we do, by restricting the matching paradigm), it is also interesting to ask what kind of other problems for a given regular expression and a string can be solved within the original matching complexity of \(O(|w|\cdot|r|)\). In this regard, our results demonstrate that in addition to checking \(w\in\mathsf{L}(r)\) there are many other relevant tasks that can be solved without an increase in complexity: checking _w_ for an infix, prefix, left-extension or extension that matches _r_, and computing a longest or shortest subsequence, supersequence, infix, prefix, left-extension or extension of _w_ that matches _r_. Furthermore, checking if all prefixes of _w_ match _r_ can also be done in quadratic time, but for infixes, this becomes cubic, while for subsequences, supersequences and extensions we even obtain intractability. The relevance of these upper bounds is also substantiated by the tight (conditional) matching lower bounds that we show to complement them.

To prove our linear upper bound for the subsequence regex matching problem, we first transform the regular expression into an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_sub that accepts the _upward closure_ of L(_r_), i.e., the set \(\{u|\exists v\in\mathsf{L}(r):v\unknown_\mathsf{sub}u\}\) (note that _w_ has a subsequence that matches _r_ if and only if \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub}))\). Similarly, the upper bound for the supersequence regex matching problem is based on constructing an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_sub for the _downward closure_ \(\{u|\exists v\in\mathsf{L}(r):v\unknown_\mathsf{sup}u\}\). The downward and upward closures are well-investigated concepts in formal language theory (see citations above). In particular, it has been noted in \[BLS15, Lemma 9\] that the powerset-DFA of _A_sub always transitions from a state set to a superset of this state set (analogously, the powerset-DFA of _A_sub always transitions from a state set to a subset of this state set). However, this property does not imply that the powerset-DFA of _A_sub and _A_sub is necessarily small, since \[Okh10\] proves an exponential lower bound on their number of states. Our notion of subsequence or supersequence matching is related to so-called _upward-closed_ and _downward-closed_ languages (which are languages equal to their upward closure or downward closure, respectively), because for such languages the usual notion of regex matching coincides with subsequence and supersequence matching, respectively. These languages have been investigated, e.g., for downward-closed languages in \[GSZ24\] or in \[ABJ98\] (under the name "simple regular expressions") and for upward-closed languages in \[GLHK<sup>+</sup>20\]. However, to our knowledge, none of the works focusing on the upward or downward closure, or on upward-closed or downward-closed languages, have investigated the complexity of the matching problem like we do. Thus it was not previously known that these problems could be solved in time _O_(|_w_|+|_r_|), or indeed that their complexity was lower than that of standard regex matching.

### 1.3 Paper Structure

In Section 2, we give preliminaries and formally define the matching problems that we study. In Section 3, we first recall some basics about the state-set simulation of \(\varepsilon\)NFAs and then explain how our regex matching problems for the subsequence and supersequence relation reduce to the state-set simulation of certain \(\varepsilon\)NFAs. Then, in Section 4, we give the corresponding linear time algorithms. Sections 5 and 6 are respectively concerned with the quantitative and universal problem variants for all considered string relations. The conditional lower bounds that complement our upper bounds are discussed in Section 7.

The present paper is the full version of the conference paper \[AMRS25\]. It includes all details and the complete proofs. Furthermore, it also contains improvements of the lower bounds for the min-variant of the subsequence matching problem, for the max-variant of the supersequence matching problem, and for the universal variant of the infix matching problem. These improvements ensure that all complexity upper bounds given in the present version of the paper are now complemented by matching lower bounds (assuming SETH).

## 2 Preliminaries and Problem Statement

### 2.1 Strings, Regular Expressions and Automata

We let \(\Sigma\) be a finite alphabet of symbols (sometimes called letters) and write \(\Sigma^*\) for the set of strings (sometimes called words) over \(\Sigma\). We write \(\varepsilon\) for the empty string. For a string \(w\in\Sigma^*\), we denote by |_w_| its length and, for every \(i\in\{1,2,\dots,|w|\}\), we denote by _w_\[_i_\] the _i_<sup>th</sup> symbol of _w_. For \(i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,|w|\}\) with \(i\le j\), we denote by _w_\[_i:j_\] the factor (also called infix) \(w[i]w[i+1]\cdots w[j]\); in particular, _w_\[_i:i_\]=_w_\[_i_\]. Further, for every letter \(a\in\Sigma\) we define \(\|w\|_a\) as the number of occurrences of letter _a_ in the string \(w\in\Sigma^*\). Lastly, we denote by \(w^R=w[|w|]w[|w|-1]\cdots w[1]\) the reverse of _w_.

_Regular expressions_ over \(\Sigma\) are defined as follows. The empty set \(\emptyset\) is a regular expression with \(\mathsf{L}(\emptyset)=\emptyset\), and every \(x\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) is a regular expression with L(_x_)={_x_}. If _s_ and _t_ are regular expressions, then \(s\cdot t\), \(s\vee t\), and _s_<sup>∗</sup> are regular expressions with \(\mathsf{L}(s\cdot t)=\mathsf{L}(s)\cdot\mathsf{L}(t)\), \(\mathsf{L}(s\vee t)=\mathsf{L}(s)\cup\mathsf{L}(t)\), and L(_s_<sup>∗</sup>)=(L(_s_))<sup>∗</sup>. Here, we define as usual: \(L_1\cdot L_2=\{uv|u\in L_1,v\in L_2\}\), \(L^0=\{\varepsilon\}\), \(L^k=L^{k-1}\cdot L\) for every \(k\ge 1\), and \(L^*=\bigcup_{k\ge 0}L^k\). The length |_s_| of a regular expression _s_ is the total number of symbols of _s_ considered as a string.

We work with _nondeterministic finite automata with_ \(\varepsilon\)_-transitions_, called \(\varepsilon\)NFA for brevity. An \(\varepsilon\)NFA is a tuple \(A=(Q,\Sigma,q_0,q_\mathsf{f},\delta)\) where _Q_ is a finite set of _states_, _q_<sub>0</sub> is the _initial state_, _q_<sub>f</sub> is the _final state_, and \(\delta\subseteq Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\times Q\) is the set of _transitions_. A transition of the form (_p,a,q_) is called an _a-transition_. We will also interpret an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_ as a graph which has vertex set _Q_ and which has directed edges labelled by symbols from \(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) given by the transitions of \(\delta\), i.e., any transition \((p,a,q)\in\delta\) is interpreted as a directed edge from _p_ to _q_ labelled by _a_. A transition (_p,a,p_) with \(p\in Q\) and \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) is called a _self-loop_. A _run_ of _A_ on an input string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) is a path (not necessarily simple) from _q_<sub>0</sub> to some state _p_ which is labelled with _w_, where the label of a path is just the concatenation of all \(\Sigma\)-labels (ignoring \(\varepsilon\)-labels). A run is _accepting_ if _p=q_<sub>f</sub>. We write L(_A_) for the _language accepted by A_, i.e., the set of all strings for which _A_ has an accepting run. The _size_ |_A_| of _A_ is its number of transitions: we usually denote it by _m_, while _n_ denotes the number |_Q_| of states.

It is well-known that a given regular expression _r_ can be converted in time _O_(|_r_|) into an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_ such that L(_A_)=L(_r_) and |_A_|=_O_(|_r_|). This can be achieved, e.g., using Thompson’s construction \[HMU01, Section 3.2.3\]. Thus, in the sequel, we assume that all input regular expressions are given as \(\varepsilon\)NFAs, and we state our results directly for arbitrary \(\varepsilon\)NFAs.

Moreover, we assume that our \(\varepsilon\)NFAs are _trimmed_, which means that every state is reachable from _q_<sub>0</sub> and every state can reach _q_<sub>f</sub>. This can always be ensured in time _O(m_). If an \(\varepsilon\)NFA is trimmed, then we also have that the number of states of the input automaton is at most twice the number of transitions plus one. We also assume that for each \(x\in\Sigma\) we have at least one transition labelled with _x_, which means that \(|\Sigma|\) is in _O(m_).

## 2.2 String Relations

A _string relation_ (_over_ \(\Sigma\)) is a subset of \(\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\). For any string relation \(\unknown\) and \(w\in\Sigma^*\) we define \(\Lambda_\unknown(w)=\{u\in\Sigma^*|u\unknown w\}\), i.e., the set of all strings that are in the \(\unknown\) relation to _w_; we also lift this notation to languages \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\), i.e., \(\Lambda_\unknown(L)=\bigcup_{w\in L}\Lambda_\unknown(w)\). Next, we define several well-known string relations.<sup>2</sup>

The _prefix_ and _infix relations_ are denoted by \(\unknown_\text{pre}\) and \(\unknown_\text{in}\): formally, we write \(u\unknown_\text{pre}w\) when _uv=w_ for some \(v\in\Sigma^*\) and we write \(u\unknown_\text{in}w\) when \(vuv'=w\) for some \(v,v'\in\Sigma^*\). The _left- extension_ and _extension relations_ are denoted by \(\unknown_\text{text}\) and \(\unknown_\text{ext}\): formally, we write \(u\unknown_\text{text}w\) when _u=vw_ for some \(v\in\Sigma^*\) and write \(u\unknown_\text{ext}w\) when \(w\unknown_\text{in}u\). The _subsequence_ and _supersequence relations_ are denoted by \(\unknown_\text{sub}\) and \(\unknown_\text{sup}\): we write \(u\unknown_\text{sub}w\) when _w_\[_j_<sub>1</sub>\]_w_\[_j_<sub>2</sub>\]_...w_\[_j_<sub>|_u_|</sub>\]=_u_ for some \(1\le j_1<j_2<\dots<j_{|u|}\le|w|\), and write \(u\unknown_\text{sup}w\) when \(w\unknown_\text{sub}u\). Note that we do not study the suffix and right-extension relations because they amount to prefix and left-extension up to mirroring the strings.

## 2.3 Problem Statement: The \(\unknown\)-Matching Problem

The well-known _regex matching_ problem is to decide whether \(w\in\mathsf{L}(r)\) for a given regular expression _r_ and input string _w_. As explained above, this generalises to the \(\varepsilon\)NFA acceptance problem, where we want to decide whether \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A)\) for a given \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_ and input string _w_. In this paper, we study the \(\unknown\)_-matching problem_, where \(\unknown\) is one of the string relations presented above: For a given string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) and an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_, decide whether _A_ accepts a string _u_ with \(u\unknown w\), i.e., decide whether \(\Lambda_\unknown(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\).

We also define _quantitative_ variants of this matching problem. For a string relation \(\unknown\), the _min-variant of the_ \(\unknown\)_-matching problem_ is as follows: For a given string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) and an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_, compute a shortest string _u_ with \(u\unknown w\) and \(u\in\mathsf{L}(A)\), or report that no such string _u_ exists. The _max-variant of the_ \(\unknown\)_-matching problem_ is as follows: For a given string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) and an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_, either report that there are arbitrarily long strings _u_ with \(u\unknown w\) and \(u\in\mathsf{L}(A)\), or compute a longest string _u_ with \(u\unknown w\) and \(u\in\mathsf{L}(A)\), or report that no such string _u_ exists. Further, all lower bounds on the quantitative variants of the matching problem will already apply in the setting where we are only required to compute the length of the witnessing string.

Finally, we define a _universal_ variant of the matching problem. For a string relation \(\unknown\), the _universal-variant of the_ \(\unknown\)_-matching problem_ is as follows: For a given string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) and an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_, decide whether _A_ matches all strings _u_ with \(u\unknown w\), i.e., decide the inclusion problem \(\Lambda_\unknown(w)\subseteq\mathsf{L}(A)\).

Finally, note that if we choose \(\unknown\) to be the string equality relation, then all the problem variants from above are just the same as the classical regex matching problem.

## 2.4 Computational Model and Basic Input-Preprocessing

The computational model we use to state our algorithms is the standard unit-cost word RAM with logarithmic word-size \(\omega\) (meaning that each memory word can hold \(\omega\) bits). It is assumed that this model allows processing inputs of size _n_, where \(\omega\ge logn\); in other words, the size _n_ of the input never exceeds (but, in the worst case, is equal to) \(2^\omega\). Intuitively, the size of the memory word is determined by the processor, and larger inputs require a stronger processor (which can, of course, deal with much smaller inputs as well). Indirect addressing and basic arithmetical or bitwise operations on such memory words are assumed to work in constant time. This is a standard computational model for the analysis of algorithms, defined in \[FW93\]. To make some of our algorithms faster, it may be necessary to allocate large arrays in constant time: for this, we use the standard technique of lazy initialisation \[GJ23\] to avoid spending linear time in the array size to initialise its cells. The time needed, after the lazy initialisation, to store a value in a cell<tbc>

In each of our problems, the input always consists of an \(\varepsilon\)NFA and a string over \(\Sigma\). As we are aiming for low complexities, it is important to define formally how the input is written: we will always assume that it obeys the following assumptions. For an \(\varepsilon\)NFA \(A=(Q,\Sigma,q_0,q_\ell,\delta)\) with |_Q_|=_n_, \(|\Sigma|=\sigma\), and \(m=|\delta|\), we assume that _Q_={1_,...,n_} and \(\Sigma=\{1,\dots,\sigma\}\); we can thus assume that both _Q_ and \(\Sigma\) are ordered sets, w.r.t. the canonical order on natural numbers. It follows that the processed strings are sequences of integers (representing the symbols), each of these integers fitting in one memory word. This is a common assumption in string algorithms: the input alphabet is said to be _an integer alphabet_ (see, e.g., \[CHL07\]). Due to the assumptions about \(\varepsilon\)NFAs made above, we also know that \(n,\sigma\) are in _O(m_). Moreover, such an automaton _A_ is given by its number of states, size of the input alphabet, initial and final state, and a list of _m_ transitions of the form \((q,a,q')\), with \(q,q'\in Q\) and \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\).

Further, using radix sort, we can prepare for each state _q_ the list _L_\[_q_\] of outgoing transitions, sorted first according to the symbol labelling them, and then by the target state; for states without outgoing transitions we set \(L[q]\leftarrow\emptyset\). This allows us to simultaneously construct, for each \(q\in Q\) and \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) for which _q_ has an outgoing _a_-transition, the list _T_\[_q,a_\] of transitions of the form \((q,a,q')\); _T_\[_q,a_\] is undefined for \(q\in Q\) and \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) in the case where _q_ has no outgoing _a_-transition. We will make the convention that, in the case that a self-loop (_q,a,q_) exists, then (_q,a,q_) is the first transition stored in _T_\[_q,a_\]; this allows us to test in _O_(1) whether there exists a self-loop (_q,a,q_) for any \(q\in Q\) and \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\). Both \(L[\cdot]\) and \(T[\cdot,\cdot]\) are implemented as arrays (of lists), which are lazily initialised (as mentioned above). So, computing the defined elements of \(L[\cdot]\) and \(T[\cdot,\cdot]\) can be done in linear time, i.e., in _O(m_).

## 3 State-Set Simulation and Simple Upper Bounds

Given a string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) and a regular expression represented as an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_, we can solve the regex matching problem of deciding whether \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A)\) using the classical approach of _state-set simulation_. It is well-known \[BI16\] that, assuming the strong exponential time hypothesis (SETH), this yields an optimal \(O(|w|\cdot|A|)\) algorithm. For our variants of regex matching, it is often possible to build an \(\varepsilon\)NFA \(A'\) from _A_ that accepts suitable strings (e.g., the subsequences or supersequences of strings of L(_A_)), so that we can solve the matching problem by checking whether \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A')\) by state-set simulation (though this is generally not optimal). Since many of our algorithms will nevertheless be specialised variants of state-set simulation, we review the technique in more detail below.

### 3.1 State-Set Simulation for \(\varepsilon\)NFA

For an NFA _A without_ \(\varepsilon\)-transitions and an input string _w_, the state-set simulation starts with _S_<sub>0</sub>={_q_<sub>0</sub>} and then, for every _i_=1,2_,...,|w_|, computes the set _S<sub>i</sub>_=C<sub>_w_\[_i_\]</sub>(_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>), where, for any state set _S_ and symbol \(b\in\Sigma\), we call C_<sub>b</sub>(S_) the set of all states that can be reached from a state in _S_ by a _b_-transition, i.e., \(\mathsf{C}_b(S)=\{q|\exists p\in S\wedge(p,b,q)\in\delta\}\). Clearly, each _S<sub>i</sub>_ contains exactly the states that are reachable from _q_<sub>0</sub> by a _w_\[1:_i_\]-labelled path. Now if we are dealing with an \(\varepsilon\)NFA, then we can use the same idea, but we also have to compute the \(\varepsilon\)_-closures_ \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(S)\) in between, i.e., the set of all states that can be reached from a state in _S_ by a path of \(\varepsilon\)-transitions. More precisely, we start with \(S_0=\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\{q_0\})\) and then, for every _i_=1,2_,...,|w_|, we compute the set \(S_i=\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\mathsf{C}_{w[i]}(S_{i-1}))\). Now each _S<sub>i</sub>_ contains exactly the states that are reachable from _q_<sub>0</sub> by a path that is labelled with _w_\[1:_i_\] (with \(\varepsilon\)-transitions being ignored in the path label). Computing _S_<sub>0</sub> is called the _initialisation_ and computing _S<sub>i</sub>_ from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> is called an _update step_ of the state-set simulation. For every _i_=0,1,2_,...,|w_|, the set _S<sub>i</sub>_ is the set of _active states at step i_. We also say that a state _p_ is _active at step i_ if \(p\in S_i\).

Given a state set _S_ and a symbol \(b\in\Sigma\), computing the set C_<sub>b</sub>(S_) can be easily done in time _O(m_), since we only have to compute for \(p\in S\) the states _q_ with a transition (_p,b,q_), which are<tbc>

given by _T_\[_p,b_\]. Thus, we have to inspect every transition at most once. Computing the \(\varepsilon\)-closure \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(S)\) can also be done in time _O(m_) by a breadth-first search (BFS) that starts in all states of _S_ and only considers \(\varepsilon\)-transitions (again, the entries \(T[p,\varepsilon]\) can be used for that). This means that the initialisation and each update step can be done in time _O(m_), which yields a total running time of _O_(|_w|m_) for the whole state-set simulation. What is more, this running time is conditionally optimal.

**Lemma 3.1** (\[BI16\])**.** _Given an_ \(\varepsilon\)_NFA A and string w, we can check in time_ \(O(|A|\cdot|w|)\) _whether_ \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A)\)_, but not in time_ \(O((|A|\cdot|w|)^{1-\epsilon})\) _for any_ \(\epsilon>0\) _unless SETH fails._

## 3.2 Solving Sub- and Supersequence Matching via State-Set Simulation

We now explain how we can use state-set simulation to solve the \(\unknown\)-matching problem for the subsequence and supersequence relations (which are our main focus in this paper). It is easy to see that we can transform an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_ into two \(\varepsilon\)NFAs _A_sub and _A_sub such that \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})\Longleftrightarrow\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\) and \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\Longleftrightarrow\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\). For example, this is done in \[BLS15, Lemma 8\]. We review this construction as we adapt it later.

The \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_sub is obtained from _A_ by simply adding a transition (_p,b,p_) for every state _p_ and \(b\in\Sigma\). Intuitively speaking, these loops equip _A_ with the general possibility to consume symbols from _w_ without transitioning in a new state, which corresponds to ignoring symbols from _w_. Hence, the "non-ignoring" transitions of an accepting run of _A_sub on _w_ spell out a subsequence of _w_ accepted by _A_. On the other hand, the \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_sub is obtained from _A_ by simply adding a transition \((p,\varepsilon,q)\) for every existing transition (_p,b,q_) with \(b\in\Sigma\). This means that while reading _w_ the automaton can always virtually process some symbols that do not belong to _w_. Hence, in an accepting run of _A_sub on _w_, the actual transitions that read the symbols from _w_ along with the added \(\varepsilon\)-transitions that virtually read some symbols spell out a supersequence of _w_ accepted by _A_.

The correctness of these constructions is shown in \[BLS15, Lemma 8\] in slightly different terms.<sup>3</sup> For the sake of self-containment, we give full proofs of their correctness below:

**Lemma 3.2** (\[BLS15\], Lemma 8)**.** _For every_ \(w\in\Sigma^*\)_, we have that_ \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})\Longleftrightarrow\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\).

_Proof._ Clearly, we have that \(\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\Longleftrightarrow w\in\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\), so it suffices to show that \(\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})=\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\) holds.

Let \(w\in\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\). This means that \(w[j_1]w[j_2]\dots w[j_\ell]\in\mathsf{L}(A)\) for some \(1\le j_1<j_2<\dots<j_\ell\le|w|\). We can accept _w_ by _A_sub by using the accepting run of _A_ on \(w[j_1]w[j_2]\dots w[j_\ell]\), but whenever we reach a position _i_ of _w_ with \(i\notin\{j_1,j_2,\dots,j_\ell\}\), we simply process _w_\[_i_\] with a loop (_p,w_\[_i_\]_,p_) of _A_sub. Thus, \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})\).

Let \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})\), i.e., _A_sub has an accepting run on _w_. Let \(w[j_1]w[j_2]\dots w[j_\ell]\) be the subsequence of _w_ where the _j<sub>i</sub>_ are exactly the positions of _w_ that _A_sub processes in its accepting run with original transitions of _A_ (i.e., not with the self-loops added to _A_ in order to obtain _A_sub). By construction, there must be an accepting run of _A_ on \(w[j_1]w[j_2]\dots w[j_\ell]\), which means that \(w[j_1]w[j_2]\dots w[j_\ell]\in\mathsf{L}(A)\) and therefore \(w\in\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\).

**Lemma 3.3** (\[BLS15\], Lemma 8)**.** _For every_ \(w\in\Sigma^*\)_, we have that_ \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\Longleftrightarrow\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\).

_Proof._ We have that \(\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(w)\cap\mathsf{L}(A)\neq\emptyset\Longleftrightarrow w\in\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\), so it suffices to show that \(\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})=\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\) holds.

Let \(w\in\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\). This means that _u=u_<sub>0</sub>_w_\[1\]_u_<sub>1</sub>_w_\[2\]_...u_<sub>|_w_|-1</sub>_w_\[|_w_\]\]_u_<sub>|_w_|</sub>\in\mathsf{L}(_A). We can accept _w_ by _A_sub by using the accepting run of _A_ on _u_, but instead of the transitions that process positions of _u<sub>j</sub>_, we simply use the corresponding \(\varepsilon\)-transitions added to _A_ in order to obtain _A_sub. Thus, \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\).

<sup>3</sup>The work \[BLS15\] is about the downward-closure and upward-closure of a language _L_, which are exactly the sets \(\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(L)\) and \(\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sup}}(L)\).

Let \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\), i.e., let _w_ be a string such that _A_<sub>sup</sub> has an accepting run on _w_. Let _u=u_<sub>0</sub>_w_\[1\]_u_<sub>1</sub>_w_\[2\]_...u_<sub>|_w_|-1</sub>_w_\[|_w_\]]_u_<sub>|_w_|</sub> be the string that we obtain by listing the transitions of this accepting run in order, substituting each \(\Sigma\)-transition (_p,b,q_) by _b_, each original \(\varepsilon\)-transition of _A_ by \(\varepsilon\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-transition that has been added due to some \(\Sigma\)-transition (_p,b,q_) by _b_ (since there might be several choices for this, we take just any of those). By construction, there must be an accepting run of _A_ on _u_, which means that \(u\in\mathsf{L}(A)\) and therefore \(w\in\Lambda_{\unknown_\mathsf{sub}}(\mathsf{L}(A))\).

Consequently, we can solve the subsequence and supersequence matching problem by checking whether \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})\) and \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\), respectively, via state-set simulation. Since \(|A_\mathsf{sub}|=O(n|\Sigma|+m)\) and |_A_<sub>sup</sub>|=_O(m_), we get the following:

**Theorem 3.4.** _The subsequence matching problem can be solved in time_ \(O(|w|(n|\Sigma|+m))\) _and the supersequence matching problem can be solved in time O_(|_w|m)._

## 3.3 Improved Algorithms for Sub- and Supersequence Matching

It has been observed in \[BLS15, Lemma 9\] that the \(\varepsilon\)NFAs _A_<sub>sub</sub> and _A_<sub>sup</sub> have special properties that can be exploited in the state-set simulations to improve the bounds of Theorem 3.4.

Firstly, for _A_<sub>sub</sub>, whenever a state _p_ of _A_<sub>sub</sub> is added to the set of active states in the state- set simulation, it will stay active until the end of the state-set simulation. This is due to the existence of the transitions (_p,b,p_) for every \(b\in\Sigma\). Consequently, for the state-set simulation of _A_<sub>sub</sub>, we have \(S_0\subseteq S_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq S_{|w|}\). Secondly, for _A_<sub>sup</sub>, we can observe that the state-set simulation starts with \(S_0=\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\{q_0\})=Q\), i.e., the set of all states, which is due to the fact that every state in _A_<sub>sup</sub> is reachable from _q_<sub>0</sub> by \(\varepsilon\)-transitions and therefore is in the \(\varepsilon\)-closure of _q_<sub>0</sub> with respect to _A_<sub>sup</sub>. Moreover, when a state _q_ is removed, it is never added back. Indeed, assume by contradiction that \(q\notin S_{i-1}\) but _q_ gets added to _S<sub>i</sub>_ by an update step. Then _q_ is not reachable from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> by \(\varepsilon\)-transitions, but it is reachable from C<sub>_w_\[_i_\]</sub>(_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>) by \(\varepsilon\)-transitions: this is impossible because in _A_<sub>sup</sub> there is a transition \((p,\varepsilon,q)\) for every existing transition (_p,b,q_) with \(b\in\Sigma\). Thus, \(S_0\supseteq S_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq S_{|w|}\).

This means that in the state-set simulation for _A_<sub>sub</sub> and _A_<sub>sup</sub> on an input string _w_, we can encounter at most _n_+1 different sets of active states. Further, for each set of active states, there are at most \(|\Sigma|\) possible update steps necessary (since if \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\mathsf{C}_{w[i+1]}(S_i))=S_i\) and _w_\[_i_+1\]=_w_\[_j_+1\] and _S<sub>i</sub>=S<sub>j</sub>_ for some _i\<j_ hold, then we do not need to update _S<sub>j</sub>_). Every actual update can again be done in time _O(m_), which yields the following:

**Theorem 3.5.** _There are algorithms that solve the subsequence matching problem in time_ \(O(|w|+n|\Sigma|\cdot(n|\Sigma|+m))\) _and the supersequence matching problem in time_ \(O(|w|+n|\Sigma|m)\).

_Proof._ According to Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3, we can solve the subsequence and supersequence matching problem by checking \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sub})\) and \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\), respectively. The proof of the theorem therefore follows from the fact that for both _A_<sub>sub</sub> and _A_<sub>sup</sub> a state-set simulation can be performed in time \(O(|w|+n|\Sigma|\cdot|A_\mathsf{sub}|)\) and \(O(|w|+n|\Sigma|\cdot|A_\mathsf{sup}|)\) instead of \(O(|w|\cdot|A_\mathsf{sub}|)\) and \(O(|w|\cdot|A_\mathsf{sup}|)\), respectively (note that _n_ is the number of states of _A_, _A_<sub>sub</sub> and _A_<sub>sup</sub>). Let us discuss this first for the case of _A_<sub>sub</sub>.

Initially, we have to compute \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\{q_0\})\), which can be done in time _O_(|_A_<sub>sub</sub>|). Now let _S_<sub>0</sub>_,S_<sub>1</sub>, _S_<sub>2</sub>_,...,S_<sub>|_w_|</sub> be the state sets of the single steps of the state-set simulation. As observed above, \(S_0\subseteq S_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq S_{|w|}\). This means that the sequence _S_<sub>0</sub>_,S_<sub>1</sub>_,S_<sub>2</sub>_,...,S_<sub>|_w_|</sub> contains at most _n_+1 distinct sets (recall that _n_ is the number of states). We say that a symbol \(b\in\Sigma\) _does not change_ a state set _S_ if \(S=\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\mathsf{C}_b(S))\). For every state set _S<sub>i</sub>_ in _S_<sub>0</sub>_,S_<sub>1</sub>_,S_<sub>2</sub>_,...,S_<sub>|_w_|</sub>, this set _S<sub>i</sub>_ is not changed by the symbols of some following update steps (possibly 0), until the state-set simulation terminates or the state set is changed to another state set.

Finding out that a symbol does not change the current state set requires time _O_(|_A_<sub>sub</sub>|), and we can then store this information. Hence, for every update step _i_, we either have to check whether _w_\[_i_\] changes _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> in time _O_(|_A_<sub>sub</sub>|), or we already know that _w_\[_i_\] does not change _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and the update step can therefore be performed in constant time. Consequently, there can be at most<tbc>

\(O(n|\Sigma|)\) update steps that require time _O_(|_A_sub|), while all other update steps can be done in constant time. This yields a total running time of \(O(|w|+n|\Sigma|\cdot|A_\mathsf{sub}|)\).

The argument for _A_sub is similar. We now have that \(S_0\supseteq S_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq S_{|w|}\), which again means that there are at most _n_+1 distinct sets of active states, and again the set of active states is not changed by the symbols of the following update steps, until the state-set simulation terminates or the state set is changed to another state set. So by the same argument as before, we conclude that there are at most \((n+1)|\Sigma|\) update steps that require time _O_(|_A_sub|), while all other update steps can be done in constant time.

We conclude the proof by observing that _A_sub has \(O(n|\Sigma|+|A|)\) transitions and _A_sub has _O_(|_A_|) transitions.

This is already a significant improvement over Theorem 3.4, since the running time is linear in |_w_|. In the next two sections, we look deeper into the problem of subsequence and supersequence matching and manage to lower its complexity to the optimum of _O_(|_w_|+_m_).

## 4 Subsequence and Supersequence Matching in Linear Time

In this section, we prove that the \(\unknown_\mathsf{sub}^-\) and \(\unknown_\mathsf{sup}^-\)matching problem can be solved in linear time _O_(|_w_|+_m_). Note that this also holds for the usual regex matching problem when the input regex or \(\varepsilon\)NFA is assumed to accept an upward-closed or downward-closed language (as matching is then equivalent to \(\unknown_\mathsf{sub}^-\) or \(\unknown_\mathsf{sup}^-\)matching). We first prove the result for the subsequence relation, which is slightly easier, and then cover the supersequence relation.

### 4.1 Subsequence Matching in Linear Time

**Theorem 4.1.** _Given a string w and_ \(\varepsilon\)_NFA A with n states and m transitions, the subsequence matching problem can be solved in time O_(|_w_|+_m)._

_Proof._ We present an algorithm to decide whether there exists a subsequence _u_ of _w_ such that \(u\in\mathsf{L}(A)\).

Let \(A=(Q,\Sigma,q_0,q_\mathsf{f},\delta)\) be the input \(\varepsilon\)NFA. For this automaton, we construct the arrays \(L[\cdot]\) and \(T[\cdot,\cdot]\) defined in Section 2. Also, we assume that every transition is initially unmarked and can be marked during the algorithm (but marked transitions stay marked and cannot be set unmarked again; intuitively, these transitions were explored in our algorithm, and do not need to be considered again). One purpose of these markings is to simplify our complexity analysis: The total running time of the algorithm will be proportional to |_w_| plus the total number of times we mark a transition. Moreover, we will repeatedly compute the \(\varepsilon\)-closure \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(S)\) of a state set _S_, but only with respect to unmarked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions, i.e., we compute \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(S)\) as discussed in Section 3, but we simply ignore marked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions, and, furthermore, while computing the \(\varepsilon\)-closure, we will mark all unmarked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions that we traverse.

We can now describe our algorithm, which is based on a state-set simulation of _A_sub, but without explicitly constructing _A_sub, i.e., we work directly on _A_. More precisely, for every _i_=0,1,2_,...,|w_|, we compute a state-set _S<sub>i</sub>_ of all states reachable from _q_<sub>0</sub> by a path labelled with a subsequence of _w_\[1:_i_\]. Additionally, we will compute (using the arrays \(L[\cdot]\) and \(T[\cdot,\cdot]\)) and maintain a lazily initialised array \(H[\cdot]\) of lists, indexed by the symbols of \(\Sigma\), such that, after _S<sub>i</sub>_ is computed, \(H[a]=\{(q,a,q')\in\delta|q\in S_i,q'\in Q,(q,a,q')\) is unmarked}\), i.e., _H_\[_a_\] contains all unmarked transitions labelled with _a_ leaving the states contained in _S<sub>i</sub>_. Moreover, as explained in Section 3, we will have \(S_0\subseteq S_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq S_{|w|}\).

We implement all the sets _S<sub>i</sub>_ with a single Boolean characteristic array _S_, which is maintained in our algorithm in such a way that _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> is the set indicated by _S_ after _w_\[_i_-1\] was processed and before the processing of _w_\[_i_\] is started, and during the processing of _w_\[_i_\] some positions of _S_ (namely, |_S<sub>i</sub>_\\_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>| many) are changed from 0 to 1. This allows us to implement in constant time the membership-testing to and insertion in the manipulated sets of states. For simplicity of the exposition, and to mirror the computation of Theorem 3.5, we use the notation _S<sub>i</sub>_ to refer to the<tbc>

<tbc>set stored in the array _S_ after the processing of _w_\[_i_\] was concluded, for all _i_ from 1 to |_w_|, and we use _S_<sub>0</sub> to refer to the content of the respective set right before we start processing _w_\[1\].

Initially, we set \(S_0=\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\{q_0\})\), where this \(\varepsilon\)-closure is computed as described above, i.e., ignoring marked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions (of which, at this step of the algorithm, none exist anyway) and marking the traversed \(\varepsilon\)-transitions. We note that this initialisation takes time proportional to the number of transitions that we mark.

Further, by traversing the lists _L_\[_q_\], for \(q\in S_0\), we can also compute, for each \(a\in\Sigma\), the list \(H[a]=\{(q,a,q')\in\delta|q\in S_0,q'\in Q\}\); note that these transitions are not marked yet, as we have only marked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions until now, and also that there are no unmarked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions leaving the states of _S_<sub>0</sub>. This takes time proportional to the sum of |_S_<sub>0</sub>| and the number of transitions inserted into the lists stored in _H_.

Let us now explain the update step, i.e., how _S<sub>i</sub>_ is computed and _H_ is updated for \(1\le i\le|w|\).

We initially set _S<sub>i</sub>=S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and let _R_ be an auxiliary empty queue, which will be used to collect all the new states from _S<sub>i</sub>_\\_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. Now, for each \((q,w[i],q')\in H[w[i]]\), we mark the transition \((q,w[i],q')\), remove it from _H_\[_w_\[_i_\]\], and, if \(q'\notin S_i\), then we add \(q'\) to _S<sub>i</sub>_ and _R_. It is worth noting that, after this loop concludes, the set _H_\[_w_\[_i_\]\] will be empty. Moreover, for all states \(q\in S_{i-1}\), there is no unmarked transition \((q,w[i],q')\) for any \(q'\in Q\). Then we compute \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(R)\), but again we ignore marked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions and mark all traversed \(\varepsilon\)-transitions. All states \(q\in\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(R)\) with \(q\notin S_i\) are added to both _R_ and _S<sub>i</sub>_. At this point, for all states \(q\in S_i\), there is no unmarked transition \((q,\varepsilon,q')\) for any \(q'\in Q\). Finally, for every \(r\in R\) and for every transition \((r,a,r')\in L[r]\) with \(a\in\Sigma\) and \(r'\in Q\), we add \((r,a,r')\) to _H_\[_a_\] (note that this transition could not have been marked before, as _r_ was not contained in any set _S<sub>j</sub>_ for _j\<i_); this step takes time proportional to the sum of |_R_| and the number of transitions inserted into the lists stored in _H_.

Once the state-set simulation is completed, we terminate and answer positively if and only if \(q_\mathsf{f}\in S_{|w|}\).

As far as the complexity of the above algorithm is concerned, we note that we have to perform _O_(|_w_|) individual updates. The total number of steps over all these updates is upper-bounded by the number of transition-insertions in the lists of \(H[\cdot]\) and transition-markings. Each transition is either never marked, or it is marked in the initialisation, where we compute \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\{q_0\})\), or it is inserted in one of the lists of the array \(H[\cdot]\) for some _i_, and then it may be marked at most once and never considered again (also, it will never be reinserted in \(H[\cdot]\) because its source state became active when the transition was inserted so the state will never be added to the queue _R_ in further update steps). Thus, our algorithm runs in _O_(|_w_|+_m_) time.

The correctness follows from the observation that our algorithm computes exactly the sets _S_<sub>0</sub>_,S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S_<sub>|_w_|</sub> of the state-set simulation with respect to the automaton _A_sub on input _w_ (see Section 3). Indeed, the set _S_<sub>0</sub> is correctly computed in the initialisation, where we also compute \(H[a]=\{(q,a,q')\in\delta|q\in S_0,q'\in Q,(q,a,q')\text{unmarked}\}\) for every \(a\in\Sigma\). Then, assuming that _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> is correctly computed and the contents of _H_ satisfy \(H[a]=\{(q,a,q')\in\delta|q\in S_{i-1},q'\in Q,(q,a,q')\text{unmarked}\}\) for every \(a\in\Sigma\), we compute _S<sub>i</sub>_ by first computing C<sub>_w_\[_i_\]</sub>(_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>) by adding all \(q'\) for every \((q,w[i],q')\in H[w[i]]\). Then we compute \(\mathsf{C}_\varepsilon^*(\mathsf{C}_{w[i]}(S_{i-1}))\) by adding the \(\varepsilon\)-closure of the states from _R_, but only with respect to unmarked \(\varepsilon\)-transitions, which is correct, since all marked transitions lead to states already in _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and can therefore be ignored. Finally, _H_ is correctly updated by adding \((r,a,r')\) to _H_\[_a_\] for every \(r\in R\) and every transition \((r,a,r')\in L[r]\) with \(a\in\Sigma\); as noted before, no transition starting in _r_ was marked, so the transitions added in this step are all unmarked, and there are no other transitions originating in _S<sub>i</sub>_ that do not already belong to the lists of _H_.

Therefore, we have shown a correct algorithm, solving the subsequence matching problem in _O_(|_w_|+_m_) time.

## 4.2 Supersequence Matching in Linear Time

The general idea is again to check \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\), and unlike in the previous subsection, we can afford to build _A_sub in time _O(m_) explicitly. However, performing a state-set simulation in linear time with _A_sub is more difficult. Intuitively speaking, in order to obtain _S<sub>i</sub>_, we have to remove<tbc>

<tbc>from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> all states that cannot be reached by any _w\[i_\]-labelled path from some other state from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. It is not directly clear how this can be done by touching each transition only a constant number of times over the whole course of the state-set simulation. One ingredient to achieve this is to first decompose _A_<sub>sup</sub> into its _strongly connected components_ (SCCs).

Recall that the _SCCs_ of a directed graph _G_ are the maximal subsets of vertices _R_ such that, for any two distinct vertices _u_ and _v_ in _R_, there is a directed path from _u_ to _v_ and from _v_ to _u_ in _G_. The SCCs of an \(\varepsilon\)NFA are simply its SCCs when seeing the automaton as a directed graph (ignoring the edge labels in \(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\)).

The _condensation_ of an \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_, denoted by `cond`(_A_), is an \(\varepsilon\)NFA whose states are the SCCs of _A_. For convenience, for every state _p_ of _A_, we denote by `SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_p_\] (or simply `SCC`\[_p_\] if _A_ is clear from the context) the SCC of _A_ that contains _p_, which, by definition, is a state of `cond`(_A_). The transitions of `cond`(_A_) are as follows: for every transition (_p,a,q_) of _A_, we have a transition (`SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_p_\]_,a,_`SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_q_\]) in `cond`(_A_). Note that `SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_p_\]=`SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_q_\] is possible, and note that several transitions may be merged in `cond`(_A_). The initial state of `cond`(_A_) is `SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_q_<sub>0</sub>\] and the final state of `cond`(_A_) is `SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_q<sub>t</sub>_\].

**Proposition 4.2.** _Given an_ \(\varepsilon\)_NFA A, we can construct `cond`_(_A_) _in time O(m)._

_Proof._ We can compute the SCCs of _A_ in time _O(m_). Now, we go over the transitions of _A_ and add the corresponding transitions to `cond`(_A_), again in time _O(m_).

Leaving aside the self-loops, the condensation of an \(\varepsilon\)NFA has the convenient property of being a directed acyclic graph (DAG). However, constructing the condensation of an automaton changes in general the language that it accepts (e.g., if _A_ can read some string _u_ by going from state _p_ to state _q_ and we have `SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_p_\]=`SCC`_<sub>A</sub>_\[_q_\], then `cond`(_A_) could read any permutation of _u_, which in general changes the accepted language). However, we shall next see that this is not the case for the \(\varepsilon\)NFA _A_<sub>`sup`</sub>, i.e., we have `L`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>)=`L`(`cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>)).

**Lemma 4.3.** _Let A be an_ \(\varepsilon\)_NFA and let_ \(w\in\Sigma^*\)_. Then_ `L`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>)=`L`(_cond(A_<sub>`sup`</sub>)).

Before proving this lemma, let us first prove an auxiliary result:

**Proposition 4.4.** _Let A be an_ \(\varepsilon\)_NFA and let C be some fixed state of `cond`_(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>)_. Assume that a string_ \(u=u[1]\cdots u[|u|]\) _can be read by `cond`_(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>)_, starting in state C and following the sequence of transitions_ (_C,u_\[1\]_,C),(C,u_\[2\]_,C),...,(C,u_\[|u|\]_,C). Then there is a path in A_<sub>`sup`</sub>_, labelled with u, between any two states of C._

_Proof._ If there is a transition (_C,b,C_) in `cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>), then there must be a transition (_p,b,q_) in _A_<sub>`sup`</sub> with \(p,q\in C\). Now let \(p',q'\) be arbitrary states from _C_. Since \(p,p',q,q'\in C\), there is a path from \(p'\) to _p_ and a path from _q_ to \(q'\) in _A_<sub>`sup`</sub> that only use states from _C_. By construction of _A_<sub>`sup`</sub>, we can further assume that these paths have only \(\varepsilon\)-transitions. Hence, we can join these two paths with the transition (_p,b,q_), which yields a path from \(p'\) to \(q'\) with exactly one non-\(\varepsilon\)-transition, which is a _b_-transition. Consequently, if `cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>) has a transition (_C,b,C_), then, for every \(p',q'\in C\), _A_<sub>`sup`</sub> has a path from \(p'\) to \(q'\) with exactly one non-\(\varepsilon\)-transition, which is a _b_-transition. This directly implies that if a string \(u=u[1]\cdots u[|u|]\) is read by `cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>), starting in state _C_ and following the sequence of transitions (_C,u_\[1\]_,C),(C,u_\[2\]_,C),...,(C,u_\[|u|\]_,C_), then there is a path in _A_<sub>`sup`</sub>, labelled with _u_ (each non-\(\varepsilon\)-transition being potentially surrounded by \(\varepsilon\)-transitions), between any two states of _C_.

Now we can give the proof of Lemma 4.3.

_Proof._ For every transition (_p,b,q_) of _A_<sub>`sup`</sub>, the transition (`SCC`\[_p_\]_,b,_`SCC`\[_q_\]) of `cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>) is called a _move-transition_ if \(\mathsf{SCC}[p]\neq\mathsf{SCC}[q]\) and a _stay-transition_ if `SCC`\[_p_\]=`SCC`\[_q_\].

Let \(w\in\Sigma^*\). Every accepting run of _A_<sub>`sup`</sub> on _w_ translates into an accepting run of `cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>) on _w_ in the following way: for every transition (_p,b,q_) of the run of _A_<sub>`sup`</sub>, we take its corresponding transition (`SCC`\[_p_\]_,b,_`SCC`\[_q_\]) in `cond`(_A_<sub>`sup`</sub>). Thus, \(\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\subseteq\mathsf{L}(\mathsf{cond}(A_\mathsf{sup}))\).

To perform a push operation with a state _q_, we simply insert _q_ at the (right) end of R, which can be done in _O_(1) time if we maintain a pointer to the respective end of R. Invariant 1 is maintained (as no change is made to the elements of \(B[\cdot,\cdot]\) and the new state _q_ is now maximal for _\<_); Invariant 2 is also clearly maintained.

For a pop operation with symbol _a_, we do the following: We traverse R from right to left until we encounter a state with _B_\[_q,a_\]=1 or we finish processing R. Now, for every state \(q\in\mathcal{R}\) with \(B[q,a]\neq 1\) which is traversed, we do the following: if _q_ does not have a self-loop labelled with _a_ then we retrieve _q_ and remove it from R, and if _q_ has such a self-loop then _q_ stays in R but we set \(B[q,a]\leftarrow 1\). This maintains Invariant 2, since we set \(B[q,a]\leftarrow 1\) only in the case that _q_ has a self-loop labelled by _a_. That Invariant 1 is maintained follows from the fact that after the pop operation, we have _B_\[_q,a_\]=1 for every \(q\in\mathcal{R}\). Indeed, after the pop, the only states of R that are still in R and have not been traversed are those states \(q'\) to the left of the rightmost state _q_ for which we had _B_\[_q,a_\]=1 before the pop (if such a _q_ does not exist then all states of R were traversed); and these states \(q'\) also had \(B[q',a]=1\) as Invariant 1 held before the current pop operation.

The total running time is proportional to the total number of operations \(\ell\), plus the total number of states traversed in pop operations. Now, every state _q_ traversed in a pop operation is either returned and removed from R, or we set \(B[q,a]\leftarrow 1\) for the symbol _a_ for which we are popping. The total number of returned states, say _r_, is upper-bounded by the total number of push operations (a state had to be pushed first for it to be removed); therefore, _r_ is in \(O(\ell)\). Now, every time we set \(B[q,a]\leftarrow 1\) for a state \(q\in\mathcal{R}\) with \(B[q,a]\neq 1\) in a pop operation, this accounts for a self-loop of _q_ labelled with _a_, and we do it only once for the pair (_q,a_). This means that the total number of these assignments is bounded by _O(m_). This concludes the complexity analysis and concludes the proof.

We will use the above structure for _A_=cond(_A_<sub>sup</sub>). We can finally show our main result:

**Theorem 4.7.** _Given a string w and_ \(\varepsilon\)_NFA A with n states and m transitions, the supersequence matching problem can be solved in time O_(|_w_|+_m)._

_Proof._ We first construct cond(_A_<sub>sup</sub>) from _A_, which can be done in time _O(m_) (see Section 3 and Proposition 4.2). As noted in Section 3, we can solve the supersequence matching problem by checking whether \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A_\mathsf{sup})\), which, by Lemma 4.3, can be done by checking \(w\in\mathsf{L}(\mathsf{cond}(A_\mathsf{sup}))\). Since |cond(_A_<sub>sup</sub>)|=_O_(|_A_|), it suffices to show that we can check \(w\in\mathsf{L}(\mathsf{cond}(A_\mathsf{sup}))\) in time _O_(|_w_|+|cond(_A_<sub>sup</sub>)|).

For convenience, we set now \(A'=\mathsf{cond}(A_\mathsf{sup})=(Q',\Sigma,q'_0,q'_\mathsf{f},\delta')\) and let \(n'=|Q'|\) and \(m'=|\delta'|\). For \(A'\), we construct the arrays \(L[\cdot]\) and \(T[\cdot,\cdot]\) defined in Section 2. We will now show how to check \(w\in\mathsf{L}(A')\) in time \(O(|w|+m')\). We will still use the special structure of \(A'\) for our algorithm, i.e., it is a DAG (potentially with self-loops) and has the property described in Proposition 4.5.

We start by pre-computing several data structures:

• \(\mathsf{loops}[\cdot,\cdot]\) is a lazily initialised \(|Q'|\times|\Sigma|\) Boolean array with \(\mathsf{loops}[q,a]=1\) if \((q,a,q)\in\delta'\).<tbc>

• L_<sub>q</sub>_ for each \(q\in Q'\) is a list that contains all \(a\in\Sigma\) with \(\mathsf{loops}[q,a]=1\).<tbc>

• \(\mathsf{in}[\cdot]\) is an array with \(\mathsf{in}[q]=|\{(q',a,q)\in\delta'|q'\in Q'\backslash\{q\},a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\}|\) for each \(q\in Q'\).<tbc>

• roots is a set with \(\mathsf{roots}=\{q\in Q'|\mathsf{in}[q]=0\}\).<tbc>

• \(\mathsf{mark}[\cdot]\) is an array with \(\mathsf{mark}[q]=0\) for all \(q\in Q'\).

Note that loops and L_<sub>q</sub>_ provide the information of which states have loops for which symbols, in\[_q_\] is the number of transitions that have _q_ as target (while originating in other states), roots stores all roots of \(A'\), and mark is a Boolean array that shall be used to mark states (initially, all states are unmarked). Note that since \(A'\) has a DAG structure, we know that \(\mathsf{roots}\neq\emptyset\).

The first three data structures can be computed simultaneously by considering every transition of \(A'\) at most once; the last two data structures can be computed by considering each state at most once. Thus, all these data structures can be computed in time \(O(m')\).

By Lemma 4.6, we can construct in time _O_(|roots|) a data structure R, storing initially the set of states in roots, and supporting the following operations:

• Push: Insert a state _q_ in R.<tbc>

• Pop: Given \(a\in\Sigma\), retrieve all states \(q\in\mathcal{R}\) such that \(a\notin\mathcal{L}_q\) and remove them from R (or indicate that no such state exists).

The initialisation of R is done by repeatedly pushing the states of roots in it. Further, the time needed by R to process a sequence of \(\ell\) push and pop operations where each state of \(A'\) is pushed at most once in total is \(O(\ell+m)\); this includes the initial push of the states in roots.

Our algorithm is an efficient implementation of the state-set simulation for the automaton \(A'\) on _w_ (see Section 3). That is, for every _i_=0,1,2_,...,|w_|, we compute a state-set _S<sub>i</sub>_ of all states of \(A'\) reachable from _q_<sub>0</sub> by a path labelled with _w_\[1:_i_\]. Moreover, since \(A'=\text{cond}(A_\text{sup})\) and Proposition 4.5 holds, we will have \(Q'=S_0\supseteq S_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq S_{|w|}\).

We implement all the sets _S<sub>i</sub>_ with a single Boolean characteristic array, which allows us to obtain _S<sub>i</sub>_ from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> by changing |_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>\\_S<sub>i</sub>_| many entries from 1 to 0 (due to the fact that \(S_{i-1}\supseteq S_i\)).

We start with \(S_0=Q'\). Recall that the data structure R contains the set of states roots.

Let us first give an intuitive explanation of how _S<sub>i</sub>_ is computed from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. Let _a=w_\[_i_\]. Since \(S_{i-1}\supseteq S_i\), we only have to identify those states that must be deleted from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> in order to obtain _S<sub>i</sub>_, which are exactly the states that cannot be reached by an _a_-labelled path from any other state of _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. Since \(A'\) has a DAG structure, this can be done as follows.

Every root without a self-loop with _a_ has to be deleted, and every root with a self-loop with _a_ will be in _S<sub>i</sub>_. In particular, we can ignore the outgoing transitions of those roots that will be in _S<sub>i</sub>_ in the rest of the update step, since they necessarily point to states that will also be in _S<sub>i</sub>_. This means that we have to be able to initially get those roots that have no self-loop with _a_, for which we employ the data structure R. Now if we remove some root _q_, then each of its outgoing transitions \((q,x,q')\) with \(x\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) has to be removed, but we also have to process each such transition as follows. If _x=a_, then \(q'\) will necessarily be in _S<sub>i</sub>_ and we do not have to consider \(q'\) again in this update step (we also mark \(q'\) accordingly). If, on the other hand, \(x\neq a\), then we first check if \(q'\) has a self-loop with _a_, which is also sufficient for \(q'\) being in _S<sub>i</sub>_ (again, we mark it accordingly and do not have to consider it again). If \(q'\) has no self-loop with _a_ and at least one other incoming transition, then we do not know whether it is in _S<sub>i</sub>_ or not, since this might be determined by some other incoming transition from a root. If \(q'\) has no self-loop with _a_, but becomes a root when we delete \((q,x,q')\), then it has to be treated as one of the initial roots (i.e., it will be deleted at some point and its outgoing transitions have to be deleted and processed as described above). In particular, this means that when we delete states and transitions, we have to update the in-degrees of states to be able to identify those states that become roots. Let us now formally define this algorithm.

We initially set \(S_i\leftarrow S_{i-1}\). Then we extract from R all states _q_ such that \(a\notin\mathcal{L}_q\) (i.e, _q_ has no self-loop with _a_) and store them in a queue _G_. While _G_ is not empty, we pop state _q_ from the queue _G_ and remove it from \(A'\) and _S<sub>i</sub>_. Then we remove from \(A'\) each transition \((q,b,q')\) with \(b\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) in _L_\[_q_\] and proceed as follows:

1. If _b=a_, then<tbc>

• set \(\text{in}[q']\leftarrow\text{in}[q']-1\);<tbc>

• set \(\text{mark}[q']=i\) (this state needs to stay in _S<sub>i</sub>_, and will no longer be analysed in this update step);<tbc>

• if \(\text{in}[q']=0\) then insert \(q'\) into R (i.e., it is now a root of \(A'\) and has to be treated like one in the next update step).<tbc>

2. If \(b\neq a\), then

• set \(\mathsf{in}[q']\leftarrow\mathsf{in}[q']-1\);<tbc>

• if \(\mathsf{loops}[q',a]=1\) then set \(\mathsf{mark}[q']=i\) (meaning that this state needs to stay in _S<sub>i</sub>_, and will no longer be analysed in this update step);<tbc>

• if \(\mathsf{in}[q']=0\) and \(\mathsf{mark}[q']=i\) then insert \(q'\) into R;<tbc>

• if \(\mathsf{in}[q']=0\) and \(\mathsf{mark}[q']\neq i\) then push \(q'\) to _G_ (this state needs to still be removed from _S<sub>i</sub>_, at a later point during the processing of _w_\[_i_\]).

Once the set _S_<sub>|_w_|</sub> is computed, we provide a positive answer to the supersequence matching problem if and only if _S_<sub>|_w_|</sub> contains the final state \(q'_\mathsf{f}\).

In order to prove the correctness of the algorithm, it is sufficient to prove that we really compute the sets _S_<sub>0</sub>_,S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S_<sub>|_w_|</sub> of the state-set simulation of \(A'\) on _w_.

Since we start with \(S_0=Q'\), this is clearly true for _S_<sub>0</sub> due to the property of Proposition 4.5. Moreover, the following invariant is satisfied: for every \(q\in S_0\), in\[_q_\] stores the number of transitions, other than self-loops, that have _q_ as target and some \(q'\in S_0\) as origin, and R stores exactly those states \(q\in S_0\) with in\[_q_\]=0.

Let us next assume that _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> has been computed correctly for some \(i\in\{1,2,\dots,|w|\}\), and that the invariant is satisfied, i.e., for every \(q\in S_{i-1}\), in\[_q_\] stores the number of transitions, other than self-loops, that have _q_ as target and some \(q'\in S_{i-1}\) as origin, and R stores exactly those states \(q\in S_{i-1}\) with in\[_q_\]=0. We will now show that _S<sub>i</sub>_ is correctly computed in such a way that the invariant is also satisfied.

Let us call every state \(q\in S_{i-1}\) _good_ if there is some state \(p\in S_{i-1}\) with a _w_\[_i_\]-labelled path from _p_ to _q_ (which can also be a self-loop); and denote states from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> as _bad_ if they are not good. This means that _S<sub>i</sub>_ is exactly the set of good states from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. Observe that if a state _q_ is good then all states that can be reached from _q_ are also good. We will show that our algorithm constructs _S<sub>i</sub>_ by deleting exactly the bad states from _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>.

Assume |_S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>|=_h_ and let us consider an arbitrary topological sorting _q_<sub>1</sub>_\<...\<q<sub>h</sub>_ of the states in _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>, w.r.t. the transitions between states of _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub> which are not self-loops. We will show, by induction on _j_, with \(1\le j\le h\), that the states removed by our algorithm from _q_<sub>1</sub>_\<...\<q<sub>j</sub>_ are exactly the bad states of {_q_<sub>1</sub>_,...,q<sub>j</sub>_}. For _j_=1, this clearly holds. Indeed, _q_<sub>1</sub> must be a root of _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>, as it comes first in the topological sorting. It is removed if and only if it has no self-loop labelled with _w_\[_i_\]; but this is equivalent to _q_<sub>1</sub> being a bad state. Assume now that our claim holds for _j_-1, and let us show that it holds for _j_. We want to show that _q<sub>j</sub>_ is removed if and only if _q<sub>j</sub>_ is bad. Assume first that _q<sub>j</sub>_ is removed by our algorithm. If _q<sub>j</sub>_ is a root of _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>, the same argument as for _q_<sub>1</sub> holds. Assume _q<sub>j</sub>_ is not a root. This means that all its parents were also removed by our algorithm (as a state _q_ is removed only if in\[_q_\]=0). But all the parents of _q<sub>j</sub>_ must come before _q<sub>j</sub>_ in any topological sorting of _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. They were removed, so they are bad states, by the induction hypothesis. Moreover, when the parents of _q<sub>j</sub>_ were removed, no _w_\[_i_\]-transition targeting _q<sub>j</sub>_ and no _w_\[_i_\]-self-loop of _q<sub>j</sub>_ were discovered. Thus, _q<sub>j</sub>_ is also bad. For the converse, assume _q<sub>j</sub>_ is a bad state. This means that all its parents (if any) are also bad. But, as before, all the parents of _q<sub>j</sub>_ (if any) must come before _q<sub>j</sub>_ in any topological sorting of _S_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. By the induction hypothesis, as they are bad, they are also removed by our algorithm. During their removal, we explore all transitions connecting them to _q<sub>j</sub>_, and this allows us to check whether there are any _w_\[_i_\]-transitions targeting _q<sub>j</sub>_ or any _w_\[_i_\]-self-loops of _q<sub>j</sub>_. The existence of such a transition would be a contradiction to the fact that _q<sub>j</sub>_ is bad. Thus, we never set \(\mathsf{mark}[q_j]\leftarrow i\), but we decrement in\[_q<sub>j</sub>_\] until it becomes 0. When this happens, _q<sub>j</sub>_ is inserted in _G_, so it will be removed. This concludes the proof of our claim. Hence, we compute _S<sub>i</sub>_ correctly.

With respect to the invariant, we observe that the values in\[_q_\] are correctly updated whenever we remove a transition, and whenever a state becomes a root, but is not removed (i.e., it will be a root in _S<sub>i</sub>_), then this state is explicitly added to R.

This concludes the proof of correctness.

As far as the complexity is concerned, the number of steps of the algorithm is proportional to the sum of |_w_|, the number of removed edges (which is \(O(m')\)), and the total time spent with the<tbc>

<tbc>data structure of Lemma 4.6. We spend time \(O(n')\) to populate it initially, and overall the number of operations performed is \(O(|w|+m')\) (and note that each state is only pushed at most once). In particular, it is important to efficiently access the roots of the DAG _S<sub>i</sub>_, and then start the exploration of _S<sub>i</sub>_ from these states; the fact that we can retrieve these states in time proportional to their number is ensured by the usage of the data structure of Lemma 4.6. Therefore, our statement holds.

## 5 Quantitative Problem Variants

For every \(x\in\{\text{in},\text{pre},\text{ext},\text{lext},\text{sub},\text{sup}\}\), we consider now the min- and max-variant of the \(\unknown_x\)- matching problem, i.e., computing a shortest or longest string \(u\in\mathsf{L}(A)\) with \(u\unknown_xw\). We show an upper bound of _O_(|_w|m_) for all these problem variants.<sup>4</sup>

**Theorem 5.1.** _The min- and max-variant of the matching problem can be solved in time O_(|_w|m_) _for all relations_ \(\unknown_x\) _with_ \(x\in\{\text{in},\text{pre},\text{ext},\text{lext},\text{sub},\text{sup}\}\).

In Section 7 we show that the _O_(|_w|m_) upper bound for all the considered variants is conditionally tight, i.e., \(O((|w|m)^{1-\epsilon})\) is not possible unless SETH fails. The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 5.1. Before giving this proof, we need some preliminaries.

Recall that a path in a directed graph may traverse the same vertex multiple times (a simple path is a path where each vertex is traversed once). An _st-path_ is a path from a vertex _s_ to a vertex _t_. When the edges of a directed graph are weighted, let weight(_e_) be the _weight_ of edge _e_ and let the weight of a path be the sum of weights of the successive edges that it traverses (if an edge is traversed multiple times then the weight is added as many times as the edge is traversed). In the case where the edges are labelled, the _label_ of a path is the concatenation of the labels of the successive edges that it traverses (if the edges carry labels in \(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\) then the label of the path is a string in \(\Sigma^*\)). We show the following ancillary result:

**Lemma 5.2.** _Let G be a directed graph with edges weighted by_ 0 _and_ 1_, and let s and t be two distinguished vertices. We can check in time O_(|_G_|) _whether there is an st-path in G, and if an st-path exists, then we can compute in time O_(|_G_|):

• _an st-path with minimum weight._<tbc>

• _whether there exist st-paths of unbounded weight in G._<tbc>

• _an st-path with maximum weight, provided that the weight of st-paths is not unbounded._

Note that the lemma is stated for edge weights 0 and 1, but applies more generally to weights bounded by a constant, as we can split every edge of weight larger than 1 into a constant number of length-1 edges connecting auxiliary nodes. Note that the lemma also applies to labelled directed graphs: in this case, when we obtain a path by applying the lemma, then we can retrieve its label (in \(\Sigma^*\)) from its sequence of edges. Let us prove the lemma:

_Proof of Lemma 5.2._ We first eliminate all graph vertices that do not have a path from _s_, as well as those that do not have a path to _t_. This is akin to automaton trimming, and can be done in _O_(|_G_|) with two graph traversals. The resulting graph is empty if and only if there is no _st_-path. Let us now assume that the trimmed graph is not empty and, for simplicity, let us denote this trimmed graph by _G_.

_Minimum weight st-path._ To compute an _st_-path of minimum weight, we simply use Dijkstra’s algorithm with a priority queue implemented with a table of |_G_| buckets. This makes it possible to insert vertices with a given priority in _O_(1), lower their priority in _O_(1), and retrieve a vertex of lowest priority in time _O_(1) per call plus an _O_(|_G_|) total cost throughout the entire algorithm<tbc>

<sup>4</sup>Of course, these upper bounds also give upper bounds on the corresponding (non-quantitative) matching problems for \(\unknown_\text{in}\), \(\unknown_\text{pre}\), \(\unknown_\text{ext}\) and \(\unknown_\text{lext}\); see  1.

<tbc>to go over successive buckets. (Note that the sequence of priorities of the vertices that we extract out of the priority queue in Dijkstra’s algorithm is nondecreasing, so we only need to go once over the sequence of buckets throughout the algorithm.) One may remark that the path of minimum weight that we obtain is always a simple path.

## Unbounded weight st-path.

To check whether there exist _st_-paths of unbounded weight, we compute the condensation of _G_ (see Section 4.2) in time _O_(|_G_|). Obviously, there is a strongly connected component (SCC) that contains an edge with nonzero weight if and only if there are _st_-paths of unbounded weight. Indeed, if there is an SCC that contains an edge with nonzero weight, then we can repeat a cycle of the SCC containing this edge as many times as we want, and combining it with a path from _s_ to the SCC and from the SCC to _t_ (these paths must exist by our preprocessing of _G_ at the beginning of the proof). On the other hand, if no such SCC with an edge of nonzero weight exists, then every possible _st_-path in _G_ has only cycles with weight-0 edges, which means that there are only a finite number of possible weights for _st_-paths.

## Maximum weight st-path.

Finally, let us assume that there are no _st_-paths with unbounded weight and let us show how to compute a largest weight _st_-path. For this purpose, we will compute a path of maximum weight that leads to _t_ from every node. However, the paths can be of linear size, so we store them in a compressed way, by remembering for every node _v_ only the first edge on a maximum weight _vt_-path. Then the path can be retrieved edge-by-edge, starting from _s_, until we reach node _t_. In addition to the first edge, we also store the total weight _X_\[_v_\] of the _vt_-path of maximum weight.

We process all SCCs of the condensation of _G_ in reverse topological ordering. Observe that within every SCC all edges have weight 0, thanks to our assumption that there are no _st_-paths with unbounded weight. First we process C_<sub>t</sub>_=SCC\[_t_\], the SCC containing _t_. Clearly, for all nodes from this component, every path to _t_ has weight 0, so we can use any such path. Now we show how to make a consistent choice of first edge towards _t_ from every node. For this, let _E<sup>rev</sup>_ be the set of all edges of C_<sub>t</sub>_, but with reversed direction, that is \(\{(q',q)|(q,q')\in E(G)\}\). We run a depth-first search from _t_ only on the nodes from C_<sub>t</sub>_, but along the reversed edges _E<sup>rev</sup>_. For every considered node \(v\neq t\), we store the edge to its parent in the recursion tree as the first edge on a _vt_-path with maximum weight. Observe that all the nodes of C_<sub>t</sub>_ will be visited, as C_<sub>t</sub>_ is a strongly connected component and so is its counterpart with edges reversed. Moreover, the chosen edges correctly define paths to _t_, as they correspond to going up the recursion tree towards the root _t_.

For every other SCC C of _G_ in reverse topological ordering, we calculate the value:

\(x:=max_{u\in\mathcal{C}}max_{(u,v)\in E(G)v\notin\mathcal{C}}\{weight((u,v))+X[v]\}\)

and we set _X_\[_u_\]:=_x_ for all \(u\in\mathcal{C}\). Note that all such edges to outside of C point to SCCs that have been already visited and hence the values _X_\[_v_\] have already been calculated for all \(v\notin\mathcal{C}\) such that there is an edge from a node from C to _v_. Let _z_ and _e_=(_z,v_) be a node and edge for which the above maximum is attained and set _e_ as the first edge on a _zt_-path with largest weight. For all nodes \(u\in\mathcal{C}\backslash\{z\}\) we find the first edge on the _ut_-path with maximum weight similarly as in C_<sub>t</sub>_, but now we start the DFS from _z_. Again, all edges within C have weight 0, so it suffices to find any path to _z_.

Finally, after processing all the SCCs, _X_\[_s_\] stores the total weight of the _st_-path of maximum weight and we can retrieve such path in linear time. This concludes the proof of the last case and hence the lemma holds.

One graph which will often be relevant is the _product graph_ of an automaton and a string:

**Definition 5.3.** _The_ product graph _G<sub>A,w</sub> of an_ \(\varepsilon NFA\) _A on states Q and a string_ \(w\in\Sigma^*\) _is the labelled and weighted graph with vertex set_ \(\{0,\dots,|w|\}\times Q\) _constructed as follows:_

• _For each transition_ \((q,\varepsilon,q')\) _in A and for each_ \(i\in\{0,\dots,|w|\}\)_, there is an edge from_ (_i,q_) _to_ \((i,q')\) _in G<sub>A,w</sub> with label_ \(\varepsilon\) _and weight_ 0.<tbc>

• _For each transition_ \((q,b,q')\) _with_ \(b\in\Sigma\) _and for each_ \(i\in\{1,\dots,|w|\}\) _with w_\[_i_\]=_b, there is an edge from_ (_i_-1_,q_) _to_ \((i,q')\) _in G<sub>A,w</sub> with label b and weight_ 1.
